answers.primary: A remote HTTP MCP server for the error-tracking vendor, added with `claude mcp add --transport http <name> <url>` and authenticated per engineer through the server's own OAuth 2.0 flow (`/mcp` inside a session, or `claude mcp login <name>` from the shell). Check the entry into a project-scoped `.mcp.json` so everyone shares the endpoint while each person's token is minted and stored individually. Claude then reads stack traces and issues as tools instead of engineers pasting them, which is the exact case the docs give for connecting a server.
answers.rejected_alternative: An HTTP server configured with a static `Authorization: Bearer` header holding a long-lived API key, the shape the docs use for GitHub. Rejected because it is one shared non-expiring credential, and because a rejected static header makes Claude Code report the connection as failed rather than falling back to OAuth.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code performs OAuth discovery, opens the browser flow, stores the token in the system keychain or credentials file, refreshes it, and retries once on a 401. The model's only role is choosing which tool to call.
answers.context_boundary: The main session. With tool search on by default only tool names and server instructions load at session start, and schemas are pulled in on demand; the stack traces themselves land in the main conversation as tool results, warned at 10,000 tokens and capped at 25,000 unless `MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS` is raised. The credential never crosses into context, but vendor-supplied text does, so treat it as untrusted input.
answers.lifecycle: The server connects at session start wherever its scope applies and reconnects with exponential backoff if it drops mid-session. The OAuth token refreshes silently until the refresh token itself is rejected, at which point `/mcp` offers Re-authenticate. It stops applying when toggled off in `/mcp`, cleared with `claude mcp logout`, or removed with `claude mcp remove`.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed: an unauthenticated server simply has no tools and shows `Needs authentication`, so Claude cannot silently proceed on stale pasted data. The practical break is non-interactive use, since `claude -p` and Agent SDK runs have no `/mcp` panel and cannot run the browser flow, so every engineer must sign in from an interactive session first.
answers.version_caveat: `claude mcp login` requires v2.1.186 or later, and its no-browser URL fallback v2.1.191; the startup notice naming servers that need sign-in requires v2.1.193; telling Claude in `-p` or SDK runs that a server's tools are unavailable until authorized requires v2.1.196 plus tool search. Use `--transport http`, since the SSE transport is deprecated.

answers.primary: An LSP server supplied by a code intelligence plugin: install `typescript-lsp` from the official marketplace, or ship your own plugin with a `.lsp.json` (or `lspServers` in `plugin.json`) mapping `.ts` and `.tsx` to `typescript-language-server`. Claude Code then pushes compiler diagnostics into context after each edit (the `diagnostics` field defaults to true) and exposes go-to-definition, find-references and hover through the LSP tool, replacing grep for symbol lookup.
answers.rejected_alternative: A `PostToolUse` hook matching `Write|Edit` that runs `tsc --noEmit` and feeds errors back. Rejected because it gives only errors, never navigation, and it retypechecks the project on every single edit instead of holding a warm incremental server.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code starts the language server subprocess, tracks edited files and injects diagnostics after each edit without being asked; the model owns only the choice to use the navigation tool instead of grep.
answers.context_boundary: The main session, but cheaply. The language server runs as its own subprocess; what crosses into context is the post-edit diagnostic list and the specific definition, reference or type answers Claude requests, which typically replaces reading whole files, so net context use can fall.
answers.lifecycle: Starts at session start once the plugin is enabled (for a project-scope skills-directory plugin, only after the workspace trust dialog), claims its declared file extensions for the session, restarts per `restartOnCrash` and `maxRestarts`, and ends at session end or when the plugin is disabled. After a mid-session plugin update, `/reload-plugins` moves it to the new path.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open and quietly, which is the trap here. The plugin configures the connection but does not ship the binary: if `typescript-language-server` is not on PATH the server is skipped, the reason appears only in the `/plugin` Errors tab as `Executable not found in $PATH`, and Claude reverts to grepping with no type errors at all. Only the first enabled server that claims `.ts` starts, so a second LSP plugin for the same extension never runs.
answers.version_caveat: The LSP tool is inactive until a code intelligence plugin is installed, and each engineer must install the language server binary separately (`npm install -g typescript-language-server typescript`). `restartOnCrash` and `shutdownTimeout` require v2.1.205 or later; before that the schema accepted them but setting either caused the server to be skipped entirely, visible only under `claude --debug`. Before v2.1.205 a server that failed to initialize still blocked another valid server for the same extension.

answers.primary: One plugin (or a small set) published through a team plugin marketplace: the review helpers as skills and agents, the reusable workflow commands as skills, the edit-time automations in `hooks/hooks.json`, and the shared external-tool configuration as the plugin's bundled `.mcp.json`. Every repository's checked-in `.claude/settings.json` then declares `extraKnownMarketplaces` pointing at the marketplace repo plus the matching `enabledPlugins` entries, so anyone who clones and trusts the folder is prompted to install the same bundle.
answers.rejected_alternative: Committing the same loose standalone `.claude/` directory (commands, agents, hooks in settings) into each repository. Rejected because there is no single source of truth and no update path: publishing a change means copy-pasting into every repo and living with the drift.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness loads and updates it, but adoption belongs to each user. Claude Code prompts at workspace trust and records the answer in user settings; short of managed settings `enabledPlugins`, nothing compels installation.
answers.context_boundary: Mixed, and that is the point of bundling. Skill and agent bodies enter the session context only when invoked or dispatched, hooks execute entirely outside the conversation and cost nothing unless they emit output, and the bundled MCP server's tools stay deferred under tool search until Claude searches for one.
answers.lifecycle: Triggered the first time an engineer trusts a repository containing the settings, then applies to every session in that repo while enabled. Updates arrive when the marketplace refreshes, automatically if the entry sets `autoUpdate: true`, otherwise on `/plugin update`. It stops applying when the user skips the prompt, sets the plugin false in `.claude/settings.local.json`, or uninstalls it.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open. An engineer who declines the prompt gets none of the helpers and nobody is notified; project `enabledPlugins` cannot install a plugin on someone else's machine, and a user-level `false` is overridden by project settings but a local-level `false` wins. Launching from a subdirectory or an untrusted folder silently yields nothing.
answers.version_caveat: As of v2.1.195 every path that loads plugins asks each user to install and trust the plugin, so a cloned repository can never push executable content unattended. `autoUpdate` defaults to false for every non-Anthropic marketplace and must be set explicitly. Administrators can block the source entirely with `strictKnownMarketplaces` or `blockedMarketplaces` in managed settings, and only managed settings can force-enable.

answers.primary: Ship the compiled CLI (or a thin per-platform wrapper for it) in the plugin's `bin/` directory. Files in a plugin's `bin/` are added to the Bash tool's PATH while the plugin is enabled, so Claude invokes it as a bare command in any Bash call, in any project, composable with grep and jq, with nobody editing their PATH.
answers.rejected_alternative: Wrapping the CLI in a bundled MCP server that exposes each subcommand as a tool. Rejected because MCP tool results cannot be piped into grep or jq inside a shell pipeline, and the requirement is explicitly shell composition rather than structured tool calls.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code injects the plugin's bin directory into the PATH of Bash tool calls whenever the plugin is enabled; the model only types the command name, and whether that call executes is then the permission system's decision, not the plugin's.
answers.context_boundary: The main session, but at near-zero cost. The binary runs inside the Bash tool's subprocess and only its stdout and stderr return as tool output. Nothing about the CLI enters context, so Claude will not know the subcommands exist unless you also ship a skill that documents them.
answers.lifecycle: On PATH for every Bash call from the moment the plugin is enabled, at session start or after `/reload-plugins`, across all projects, and gone the moment the plugin is disabled or uninstalled. A plugin update relocates `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}`, so anything the binary writes must not live beside it.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed but disguised as an ordinary shell error: with the plugin disabled, the file not marked executable, or the wrong build installed, Claude sees `command not found` and typically improvises another route rather than reporting that the toolkit is missing. A single committed binary is also OS and architecture specific, so a mixed macOS, Linux and Windows fleet needs per-platform builds or a wrapper that resolves them.
answers.version_caveat: The `bin/` PATH injection is listed as a standard plugin component in this documentation set with no stated minimum version, plan restriction, or enabling flag. Two constraints do apply: an installed plugin cannot reference files outside its own directory, since marketplace plugins are copied into `~/.claude/plugins/cache` and traversing paths such as `../shared` are not copied; and symlinks in `bin/` that resolve outside the marketplace are skipped for security.

answers.primary: Distribute the bundle as a plugin from a git-hosted marketplace and use commit-SHA versioning: leave `version` unset in both `plugin.json` and the marketplace entry so Claude Code falls back to the git commit SHA of the plugin's source, and set `"autoUpdate": true` on the marketplace entry so Claude Code refreshes the marketplace and updates installed plugins in the background after startup. Every merged commit then counts as a new version with no release step.
answers.rejected_alternative: Setting an explicit semantic `version` in `plugin.json` and bumping it per release. Rejected because it is precisely the bookkeeping they want gone: pushing commits without bumping ships nothing and `/plugin update` reports the plugin is already at the latest version.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code resolves the version, uses it as the cache key, decides whether an update is available and pulls the new copy into the plugin cache on its own.
answers.context_boundary: None of this touches the model's context. The marketplace refresh and cache copy are harness work in the background after startup; only the updated components' content appears in a later session's context when a skill is invoked or a hook returns output.
answers.lifecycle: Runs on the post-startup background refresh once `autoUpdate` is on, or manually via `/plugin update`. Each version lands in its own cache directory and the previous directory is marked orphaned and removed 14 days later, so concurrent sessions on the old version keep working. A mid-session update does not take effect until `/reload-plugins`, and monitors need a full session restart.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open and fast: there is no gate between a merge and every teammate's machine, so a broken commit becomes a broken toolkit fleet-wide by the next session. The likeliest silent failure is forgetting `autoUpdate`, which defaults to false for non-Anthropic marketplaces and leaves everyone pinned to whatever they installed. Commit-SHA versioning also only exists for git sources; npm sources and local directories outside a git repo resolve to `unknown` and never look updated.
answers.version_caveat: The commit-SHA fallback applies to `github`, `url`, `git-subdir` and relative-path sources inside a git-hosted marketplace. `plugin.json`'s `version` wins over the marketplace entry, so a leftover `version` field in either place silently reinstates manual bumping. `skipLfs` on the source requires v2.1.153 or later, and `claude plugin prune` for orphaned dependencies requires v2.1.121.

answers.primary: An HTTP MCP server entry whose credential comes from `headersHelper` pointed at the SSO helper command, for example `"headersHelper": "/opt/bin/get-mcp-auth-headers.sh"`. Claude Code runs that command at connection time and merges its JSON stdout into the request headers, so each connection carries a freshly minted short-lived token without the service needing OAuth endpoints. The docs name exactly this case: Kerberos, short-lived tokens, or an internal SSO.
answers.rejected_alternative: A static `headers.Authorization` bearer value, optionally via `${VAR}` expansion of an env var holding the token. Rejected because that value is fixed when the configuration loads and cannot be re-minted when the token expires part-way through a session.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code executes the helper in a shell, merges its output over any static headers, and from v2.1.193 re-runs it, reconnects and retries once when a tool call returns 401 or 403. The model never sees or handles the credential.
answers.context_boundary: The token stays out of the model's context entirely: the helper runs in a shell subprocess with a 10-second timeout, from the session's working directory (or the plugin root for a plugin-provided server), and only the resulting tool results cross into the session.
answers.lifecycle: The helper runs fresh on every connection, at session start and on each reconnect, with no caching at all, so any token reuse is the script's own responsibility. It also runs on the automatic re-run after a 401 or 403. It stops applying when the server is toggled off in `/mcp` or removed.
answers.failure_mode: Mostly fails closed, with one real gap: because the helper fires only at connect time, a token that expires between reconnects produces a failing tool call, and only from v2.1.193 does that 401 or 403 trigger a re-run plus one retry. If the retry also fails, the server is flagged as needing authentication in `/mcp`. A helper that overruns 10 seconds or prints anything other than a JSON object of string pairs fails the connection outright.
answers.version_caveat: Automatic re-run and single retry on 401/403 requires v2.1.193 or later. For a plugin-provided server, `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` substitution inside `headersHelper` and the plugin-root working directory require v2.1.195 (before that the placeholder was passed through literally). From v2.1.207 a plugin `headersHelper` cannot reference `${user_config.*}` because the command runs through a shell, so pass such values in `headers` or have the script read them from a config file. At project or local scope the helper executes only after the workspace trust dialog is accepted.

answers.primary: A background monitor declared by the plugin, in `monitors/monitors.json` at the plugin root (or `experimental.monitors` in `plugin.json`): an entry such as `{"name": "error-log", "command": "tail -F ./logs/error.log", "description": "Application error log"}` with the default `"when": "always"`. Claude Code starts it automatically whenever the plugin is active and delivers every stdout line to Claude as a notification for the whole session.
answers.rejected_alternative: Letting Claude call the Monitor tool itself when it decides a watch is useful. Rejected because that requires someone to ask, which is the one requirement stated: the watch must start without anyone requesting it.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code spawns the process at session start, owns it for the session's lifetime and pushes each line in as a notification; nothing depends on the model choosing to watch or remembering to keep watching.
answers.context_boundary: The lead session's main context: each stdout line becomes a notification in the conversation, so a chatty log spends context continuously for the entire session. The process itself runs outside the conversation, unsandboxed in the session working directory at the same trust level as hooks.
answers.lifecycle: Starts at session start and again on plugin reload with `when: "always"`, runs as a persistent background process for the session, and notably does not stop if you disable the plugin mid-session: it ends only when the session ends. Picking up a monitor command changed by a plugin update needs a full session restart, not just `/reload-plugins`.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open and silently. Monitors run only in interactive CLI sessions, are skipped on hosts where the Monitor tool is unavailable, and are not loaded at all by a project-scope skills-directory plugin, so Claude simply never hears about the log and no one is told why. In the opposite direction a high-volume error log floods the conversation with notifications and crowds out real work.
answers.version_caveat: Monitors are an experimental plugin component whose manifest schema may change between releases; declare them under `experimental.monitors`, since the top-level key still loads but `claude plugin validate` warns and a future release will require the nested form. From v2.1.207 a monitor `command` cannot reference `${user_config.*}` (Claude Code rejects the monitor rather than substituting), and monitor processes do not receive `CLAUDE_PLUGIN_OPTION_<KEY>` variables, so the script must read such values from a config file it owns.

answers.primary: Pin the scope set on the MCP server entry: `"oauth": {"scopes": "<the read-only scopes>"}` in the server's configuration. The docs name this as the supported way to restrict a server to a security-team-approved subset when the upstream authorization server advertises more scopes than you want to grant, and it is a single space-separated RFC 6749 scope string. The credential each engineer's browser flow mints is then issued without write or admin scope.
answers.rejected_alternative: Permission deny rules on the vendor's write tools, for example `permissions.deny` entries matching `mcp__vendor__*write*`. Rejected because that only stops Claude Code from calling them; the token sitting on the engineer's machine would still authorize a write, which is exactly the distinction the security team drew.
answers.enforcement_owner: Neither the model nor, ultimately, the harness: the vendor's authorization server is what mints a token that lacks write scope. Claude Code's role is to request the pinned set rather than the discovered catalog, so the guarantee lives on the credential itself and holds even outside Claude Code.
answers.context_boundary: Configuration rather than context. The pinned scopes sit in the server entry, the resulting token in the OS keychain or `~/.claude/.credentials.json`, and neither is ever visible to the model; only tool results cross into the session.
answers.lifecycle: Applied during the authorization flow, so it takes effect at first sign-in and on every re-authentication. A 403 `insufficient_scope` from a tool call causes Claude Code to re-authenticate with the same pinned scopes rather than widening them. It stops applying only when someone edits or removes `oauth.scopes`, at which point the next sign-in can mint a broader token.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed by design: any tool needing a scope outside the pin is refused by the vendor with 403 `insufficient_scope`, and Claude Code will not escalate on its own. The practical hazards are that `oauth.scopes` takes precedence over both `authServerMetadataUrl` and `/.well-known` discovery, so a read scope you forgot to list is also blocked; that Claude Code appends `offline_access` when the server advertises it; and that a user-editable local or user-scope entry lets an individual undo the pin, so place it where they cannot, such as managed settings or managed MCP configuration.
answers.version_caveat: From v2.1.196, with `oauth.scopes` unset Claude Code requests only the scope from `WWW-Authenticate` or protected resource metadata instead of the whole `scopes_supported` catalog; requesting that catalog is what previously pulled in admin-only scopes and produced `invalid_scope` rejections. Note also that metadata fetched from a configured `authServerMetadataUrl` still supplies its `scopes_supported`. If this vendor is reached as a claude.ai connector rather than a Claude Code server entry, `oauth.scopes` does not apply and the equivalent lever is your organization's per-tool `blocked` setting, enforced from v2.1.129.

answers.primary: A project-scoped MCP server checked into the repository root as `.mcp.json`, added with `claude mcp add --transport http staging-db --scope project <url>` (or the stdio equivalent). Project scope loads only in that project, travels with a fresh clone through version control, and Claude Code prompts each person for per-server approval before it is ever used.
answers.rejected_alternative: User scope (`--scope user`, stored in `~/.claude.json`). Rejected on both halves of the requirement: a user-scoped server loads in all of that person's projects, and it does not arrive with a fresh clone, so each new teammate would have to add it by hand.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code reads `.mcp.json`, gates it behind the workspace trust dialog and the per-server approval prompt, and records each user's decision in settings rather than leaving it to the model.
answers.context_boundary: The main session. Tool schemas stay deferred under tool search until Claude searches for one, and query results enter the main conversation subject to the 10,000-token warning and 25,000-token default cap. Note the precedence order: a local-scope entry of the same name in `~/.claude.json` would win over the committed one.
answers.lifecycle: Evaluated at every session start in that repository. Consent is asked once per person and persists; `claude mcp reset-project-choices` clears it, `disabledMcpjsonServers` rejects the server permanently, and toggling it off in `/mcp` disables it per project without deleting the configuration.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed, in a way that reads like a broken repo. Until the person runs `claude` interactively in the folder and accepts the workspace trust dialog, the server sits at `Pending approval (run claude to approve)` and its tools do not exist; `claude mcp list` shows it there too. As of v2.1.196 a committed `enableAllProjectMcpServers` or `enabledMcpjsonServers` in the project's own `.claude/settings.json` is ignored in an untrusted folder, so the repository deliberately cannot pre-approve itself.
answers.version_caveat: An entry that has a `url` but no `type` is a configuration error and the server is skipped, since Claude Code reads a typeless entry as stdio; before v2.1.202 this surfaced as the confusing `command: expected string, received undefined`. The untrusted-folder approval rules require v2.1.196 or later, and from v2.1.207 approvals in an untracked `.claude/settings.local.json` also wait for the trust dialog. WebSocket servers, if you chose that transport, do not appear in `claude mcp list` at all.

answers.primary: A `SessionStart` hook in the plugin that installs into `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}`, the plugin's persistent data directory at `~/.claude/plugins/data/{id}/`, which is created on first reference and survives plugin updates. The documented pattern diffs the bundled `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/package.json` against a copy stored in the data directory and re-runs `npm install` there when they differ; bundled scripts and the plugin's MCP server then point at it with `NODE_PATH=${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}/node_modules`.
answers.rejected_alternative: Running the same install into `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}`, the plugin's installation directory. Rejected because that path changes on every plugin update and the old version directory is marked orphaned and cleaned up about two weeks later, so the modules are stranded with the version that installed them, which is the exact failure the requirement names.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. The hook fires on the `SessionStart` event and runs as a command in its own process; the model is not involved, cannot skip it, and does not have to remember to bootstrap anything.
answers.context_boundary: Outside the conversation. The hook executes at session start and contributes nothing to context unless it prints output; the installed modules live on disk in the data directory, shared across every session and every future version of the plugin.
answers.lifecycle: Fires at every session start and resume, no-ops when the stored manifest matches the bundled one, and reinstalls whenever an update changes `package.json`. The data directory outlives every plugin version and is deleted only when the plugin is uninstalled from its last remaining scope, unless you pass `--keep-data`; the `/plugin` interface shows its size and prompts first, while the CLI deletes by default.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open. If `npm install` fails (offline machine, private registry, no node) the session still starts and the plugin is simply broken at its first call. That is why the documented command ends with `rm -f "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}/package.json"`: removing the copied manifest makes the next session retry instead of believing it is installed. The classic bug is checking only whether the directory exists, which silently keeps stale modules after a dependency-changing update, so the manifest comparison is the load-bearing part. The first session on each machine also pays the install latency.
answers.version_caveat: `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}` appears in this documentation set as a standard plugin path placeholder with no stated minimum version, plan restriction, or enabling flag, and it resolves in hook, monitor, MCP and LSP configurations alike. The timing caveat is what bites: a plugin that updates mid-session keeps hooks, MCP servers and LSP servers on the previous version's `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` until `/reload-plugins`, and monitors until a session restart, so a hook that just installed against the new manifest can briefly be paired with old code.
